title: GPU profiling and tracing
subtitle: I instrument ActiveKV down to the runtime call level and I measure the instrument: a profiler that serialised the copy engine it was observing got its verdict retracted in the plan.

stats.label: capture levels, from runner phases to every runtime call
copy overlap at best with timing events on, down to 0.02
the same overlap at best with them off, down to 0.79

lede: ActiveKV is only faster if I can see where each decode step spends its time, on the host and on the device, and the act of looking changes the answer. I decided to build the instrument and then measure the instrument. I directed the build of a step-profiling suite with capture levels chosen per run. Readers sit on top of the captures. The token-life view follows every generated token from the scheduler through each device milestone to the client. I keep association and causation apart, and I treat an idle-looking queue as a question about the hardware. Each chart prints its own uncertainty, including the unproven device-to-host clock conversion. Two problems shaped the suite.
quote: I removed automatic verdicts from the comparison output, because a profiler should collect and the engineer should judge.
evidence: GPU profiling and tracing: a step profiler for ActiveKV on Intel Arc with 4 capture levels, from runner phases to every Unified Runtime call, and token-life views from scheduler to client.
Measurement integrity: a profiler shown to serialise the copy engine, with copy overlap 0.02 to 0.21 with timing events on against 0.79 to 1.09 off, and the verdict retracted.
LD_PRELOAD symbol interposition: runtime calls intercepted by a flat-memory shim when the vendor tracing path leaked, so several captures could run at once.
author: Corey James
